pairs.floor: copy five columns onto the stored object, one store each
pairs.caveat: THE FLOOR CANNOT EXPRESS ONE HALF OF WHAT UPSERT PROMISES. An upsert of an existing key also REMOVES the columns the new value does not carry, which means walking the stored row to find them; here both rows carry all five columns, so that walk finds nothing and the floor's five stores are the same net effect. Ours additionally gates each column on the default equality, so only the column that actually moved is written and reported, where the floor writes all five every time. THAT DEFAULT IS SAMEVALUEZERO AND WAS AN INLINE `===` WHEN THIS ROW WAS RECORDED: the four columns this fixture does not move settle on the first clause and cost what they cost before, and the one that moves carries one comparison this figure never saw. Direction: mixed — the gate saves us four stores and costs us five comparisons plus a moved-list allocation, and the marking and routing are ours alone. Read it beside update.column: the difference between the two is what sending a whole row costs over sending the column that changed. THE STRUCTURAL CAVEAT AT THE HEAD OF THIS REPORT RUNS BACKWARDS ON THIS ROW AND ON NO OTHER WRITE ROW. It says a Map-keyed floor pays a hash our identity path does not, which flatters us. Here it is the reverse: the floor is handed `held[i]` by its index and never looks anything up, while ours is handed a ROW and must resolve its key — `keyOf` and then the store lookup inside `writeContentByKey`, a `Map.get` over eight thousand string keys. That lookup is inside our number and outside the floor's, so this row overstates what the design costs a caller who already holds the identity. `upsert.whole-row-vs-map-get-and-five-stores` is the same measurement with the lookup on both sides; the difference between the two rows is the hash, and neither alone is the price of an upsert.

pairs.floor: walk the stored row for columns the new one does not carry, then five stores
pairs.caveat: THE DEPARTURE WALK, PUT ON THE FLOOR, WHICH IS THE ONLY WAY THIS HARNESS CAN PRICE AN OPERATION THAT NEITHER ARM OF AN EXISTING ROW ISOLATES. `upsert.whole-row-vs-five-stores` charges our side a walk of the STORED row's own names, with a `hasOwnProperty` probe of the caller's row per name, and its floor makes neither — so the walk sits inside that row's residual with the marking, the routing and four extra columns of comparison, and nothing separates it from them. Here the floor makes the identical walk, to the line of `OIMEntityCollection.writeEntity`, and stores five columns after it. THE ITEM IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THIS ROW'S GAP AND THAT ROW'S GAP, and nothing else about either arm changes. OUR ARM IS THAT ROW'S ARM TO THE CHARACTER — the same fixture, the same two whole-row variants alternating so `title` moves on every row of every pass, the same flush per eight thousand writes, the same absence of an index, a subscriber and a projection. So the two rows' `ours` columns should agree to within the between-pair disagreement of this piece, and a run where they do not is a run that has said something about the machine rather than about the walk. OPERATION COUNT, THE DIFFERENCE ONLY: one `for…in` over the five names the stored row carries, five `hasOwnProperty` probes of a five-property row, and one `??=` test that never fires — both rows of this fixture carry all five columns, so nothing ever leaves and no array is allocated on either arm. That is the walk at its CHEAPEST: it finds nothing, which is what a server re-sending whole rows always makes it do, and it is the case an upsert being a whole-row replace is charged for. A payload that genuinely drops a column would add a push, a `deleteColumns` call and an `undefined` write per departing name to our side and a `delete` to the floor. WHAT THIS ROW IS NOT. It is not a merge-versus-replace comparison — the floor here is not the rejected design, it is the shipped design with one item lifted out of it and set beside a hand-written store. The rejected design is `upsertEntity` WITHOUT the walk, which is `upsert.whole-row-vs-five-stores` with a floor that does less, and no row in this suite is that. Read this one as the price of the item, not as a verdict on the consequence.

pairs.caveat: THE ROW ABOVE, WITH THE LOOKUP PUT BACK ON THE FLOOR. `upsertEntity` is handed a ROW and not an identity, so it calls `keyOf` and then `writeContentByKey` — a `Map.get` over eight thousand string keys — before it can write anything. The floor of `upsert.whole-row-vs-five-stores` is handed `held[i]` by its loop index and never looks anything up, which makes that row the one write row in this suite where the hash falls on OUR side. Here the floor resolves the same key through its own `Map` first, so both sides pay one hash and the row is what a person doing this job by hand would actually have written. OUR SIDE IS THE SAME BODY AS THE ROW ABOVE, deliberately and to the line: the same fixture, the same two whole-row variants alternating so the title moves on every row of every pass, the same flush per eight thousand writes. Nothing about our arm differs, so the two rows' `ours` columns should agree to within the between-pair disagreement of this piece, and the difference between the two FLOORS is one `Map.get` and one `undefined` test. READ THE PAIR OF ROWS, NOT EITHER ONE: the row above prices an upsert against a floor that already knows where the row is, this one against a floor that has to find out, and a caller sits at one or the other depending on whether the write came from a socket payload or from something they were holding. WHAT IS STILL NOT EQUAL. The floor's five stores are unconditional where ours gates each column on the default equality — SameValueZero — and writes the one that moved; ours walks the stored row for columns the new value does not carry (here it finds none, so the net effect matches); and the marking, the presence of a `columnSlotStoreService.get` probe per moved column and the frame that closes the batch are ours alone. All three are stated on the row above and are unchanged by moving the lookup — this row changes exactly one thing about that comparison, which is the point of it.
